strengths: The paper extends the function vector framework from LLMs to a multimodal model (OpenFlamingo-4B) for spatial relational reasoning, a genuinely underexplored setting, and uses a principled causal mediation analysis (AIE) to identify attention heads rather than relying on correlational evidence.

The experimental pipeline is reasonably comprehensive for a proof of concept: head identification, zero-shot injection, fine-tuning of the function vectors with the backbone frozen, and composite function vectors for untrained relations (one-shot analogies), plus ablations on injection layer, head set size, and context size.

The composite function vector experiment is the most original part: showing that relation-specific vectors can be linearly combined to solve analogies for relations never seen in training provides evidence for a form of linear relational structure in an LMM.

Dataset construction (synthetic images with controlled spatial layouts and a curated GQA subset) is described in detail, ablation results are provided in the supplement, and the authors include an ethics statement, reproducibility statement, and an anonymous code/data repository.
The limitations section is honest and specific: single architecture, lightweight model, and a narrow set of spatial relations.
weaknesses: Absolute performance is very low throughout (e.g., fine-tuned FV accuracy of roughly 0.2–0.3 on synthetic data, ~0.5 in some GQA conditions, and 16.8% vs. 8.3% for CFVs in the analogy task), so the headline claim that fine-tuned vectors 'significantly outperform' baselines rests on modest margins over near-chance baselines, and no statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or error bars are reported anywhere despite repeated use of the word 'significantly'.

The comparison between fine-tuned function vectors and in-context learning baselines is not apples-to-apples: the FVs are fine-tuned on task-specific supervised data (1000 zero-shot examples), while ICL baselines use no training data. Missing baselines such as a linear probe on the same hidden states, LoRA/adapter fine-tuning of comparable capacity, or random-vector controls would be needed to establish that the gains come from the extracted relational representation rather than from any injected vector optimized on the objective.

Novelty is incremental relative to existing work: Multimodal Task Vectors (Huang et al., 2024) and Visual Task Vectors (Hojel et al., 2024) already establish task-vector extraction in multimodal models; the paper does not directly compare against these methods even though they are the closest prior work.
The evaluation uses a single, small model (OpenFlamingo-4B), which the authors acknowledge; generalization claims about 'LMMs' in the abstract and conclusion are therefore overbroad.
The GQA evaluation relies on only 201 images (101 train / 100 test) selected by strict criteria, raising concerns that the real-image results are unrepresentative and fragile.

Internal inconsistencies and presentation problems reduce confidence: Equation 2 defines the function vector as a sum while the text says 'averaging the activations'; the injection layer is 19 for synthetic data but 8 for GQA without a satisfying explanation; several typos ('approch', 'illusation', 'MOELS', 'two rans'); and several figures (AIE heatmaps, accuracy line plots) are too small to read.

The analogy/CFV experiment lacks analysis of failure modes and chance baselines: with four candidate relations and weighted combinations of only four vectors, it is unclear how much of the 16.8% accuracy reflects genuine compositional structure versus artifacts of the weighting scheme; no random-weight or shuffled-vector control is provided.

strengths: The core question—whether function vectors extend to multimodal models for visual relational knowledge—is well-motivated and connects mechanistic interpretability with spatial reasoning in LMMs.

The experimental pipeline is coherent: causal mediation analysis (AIE) to identify attention heads, FV extraction, zero-shot intervention, FV fine-tuning, and composite vectors for analogy tasks form a logical progression, following a sound methodology from Todd et al. (2024).
Both synthetic and real-image (GQA) data are used, and ablations over injection layer, head-set size, and context size are provided in the supplementary material.

Reproducibility is addressed well: detailed dataset construction criteria, hyperparameters (Adam, lr, epochs, injection layers), an anonymous OSF repository with code and data, and honest limitations and ethics statements.
weaknesses: Limited originality: the paper is essentially a direct transplant of the function-vector recipe (Todd et al., 2024) and MTV-style analysis (Huang et al., 2024) to OpenFlamingo-4B with spatial relations. The closest related work (Multimodal Task Vectors) is cited but never empirically compared against, leaving the delta over prior multimodal task-vector work unclear.

Methodological inconsistency: Equation (2) defines the function vector as the SUM of mean activations from selected heads, but Section 4.1 states it is 'calculated by averaging the activations from the selected top 10 heads.' This discrepancy matters because scaling affects the additive intervention in Eq. (3), and it undermines confidence in the reported results.

The central comparative claim—that fine-tuned FVs 'significantly outperform' all baselines—is not uniformly supported: in Figure 5(d) for GQA, 4-shot ICL appears to beat the fine-tuned FV for 'above' (≈0.30 vs ≈0.24). No statistical tests, confidence intervals, or multiple seeds are reported anywhere despite repeated claims of 'significant' improvements.

Absolute performance is very low (e.g., fine-tuned FV accuracy ~0.2–0.3 on synthetic data; 16.8% on analogy tasks), and chance levels are never stated, making it hard to judge whether the gains are meaningfully above random guessing (especially for the 4-way analogy task).

The analogy/composite-vector analysis does not convincingly support the 'linear combination of relation vectors' claim: the reported weights (e.g., 0.52 and 0.39 on two vectors) suggest near-selection of a single dominant vector via a softmax over model probabilities, which is a soft retrieval mechanism rather than evidence of compositional linear structure of untrained diagonal relations.

Scale and generality concerns: a single, relatively weak model (OpenFlamingo-4B with a 3B RedPajama backbone), only 201 GQA images, and 32 synthetic object cutouts. The synthetic layout (four objects at fixed cardinal positions) makes the task trivially structured, so results may not transfer to natural scenes. The authors acknowledge this, but it substantially limits the contribution's reach.

Ad hoc and under-justified design choices: fine-tuning uses layer 19 for the synthetic set but layer 8 for GQA with no explanation, and top-10 heads are selected without cross-validated justification; the first-token top-1 accuracy metric is crude and sensitive to tokenization of object labels.

Missing baselines: no comparison to prompt tuning, a linear probe on hidden states, or MTV extraction on the same data, so it is impossible to determine whether the causal-mediation head selection is actually necessary versus simply fine-tuning an arbitrary vector at layer 19.

Presentation quality is below the bar for a main-track submission: numerous typos ('approch,' 'illusation,' 'MOELS,' 'rans,' 'lable,' 'relation-secific'), Eq. (4) notation is ill-formed, and key quantitative results are relegated to hard-to-read supplementary heatmaps and bar plots without numeric tables.

strengths: The paper extends the function vector framework from LLMs to vision-language models for a genuinely understudied problem (spatial relational knowledge), combining causal mediation analysis, inference-time intervention, FV fine-tuning, and linear composition into a coherent pipeline.

Both a controlled synthetic dataset (enabling precise causal analysis and a clean generalization test with diagonal relations) and a real-image GQA dataset are used, and dataset construction is described in detail in the supplementary material.

Useful ablation studies on injection layer, head-set size, and context size, showing a non-monotonic head-count effect (peak at 6-12 heads) and intermediate-layer optimality; these are informative for future work on localized task representations.
The composite function vector experiment on untrained diagonal relations is a novel and interesting test of the linear representation hypothesis in a multimodal setting.

The paper is honest about its limitations (single, relatively small architecture; restricted set of spatial relations), provides ethics and reproducibility statements, and reports an anonymous code/data repository.
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to prior work: the core machinery (AIE-based head selection, FV extraction via attention-head activation averaging, injection at intermediate layers) is directly transferred from Todd et al. (2024), and multimodal task-vector extraction in OpenFlamingo-style models already exists (Hojel et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2024). The genuinely new elements are the spatial-relation focus, FV fine-tuning, and composite vectors, and the paper should more sharply delineate its delta over Huang et al.'s Multimodal Task Vectors.

Absolute performance is low and chance levels are never stated: fine-tuned FVs reach roughly 0.25-0.27 accuracy on synthetic data and CFVs reach 16.8% on analogy tasks. Without a chance baseline (e.g., uniform over candidate objects or first-token frequency), it is hard to judge how far these numbers are above random guessing, and claims of 'nearly doubling' accuracy are made from a very low base.
No statistical rigor: 'significantly outperform' is claimed repeatedly (e.g., Figures 5 and 6) but no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests over tasks/seeds are reported.

The fine-tuning comparison is not fully apples-to-apples: the FV is optimized on 1,000 zero-shot examples while the ICL baseline sees only 4 demonstrations. A parameter-efficient fine-tuning baseline (e.g., LoRA or LoFit, which they cite) trained on the same data would be needed to substantiate the claim that FVs are a preferable control mechanism.

The composite-vector analysis is thin: with only four basis vectors and softmax-normalized weights, it is unclear whether CFVs do more than softly select the nearest relation vector; a baseline using only the highest-weight vector, or random weightings, is missing, and the analogy evaluation is done only on synthetic data.

Inconsistencies and polish issues: Eq. (2) defines v_t as the sum of mean activations while Section 4.1 says it is 'calculated by averaging'; the choice of layer 19 for synthetic data but layer 8 for GQA fine-tuning is unexplained; and the manuscript contains multiple typos ('approch', 'illusation', 'rans', 'secific', 'MOELS', 'multimod').

All conclusions rest on a single, relatively dated, 4B-scale model (OpenFlamingo-4B with RedPajama-3B); generalization to modern LMM architectures with different fusion mechanisms is left open, which limits the significance of the 'localized relational knowledge' claim for state-of-the-art models.

strengths: The paper extends the function vector framework (Todd et al., 2024) from LLMs to large multimodal models, focusing on visual spatial and agentic relations, a setting not previously covered by multimodal task vector work (Hojel et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2024), providing a reasonable and clearly motivated contribution.

The methodology is a faithful adaptation of causal mediation analysis with appropriate controls: perturbed 'uninformative context' prompts are carefully constructed so that all relation types appear equally often, avoiding label-bias confounds in the AIE computation.

Evaluation spans both a controlled synthetic dataset and real-image GQA spatial/agentic data, two architecturally different models (OpenFlamingo and Qwen3-VL), and multiple held-out test sets (novel objects, novel relations, cross-dataset transfer), giving the core claims decent empirical breadth.

Thorough ablations cover injection layer (non-monotonic peak at intermediate layers), head set size (sparse optimum of 6-12 heads), and context size, and the appendix reports per-relation results, AIE heatmaps for all relations, and cross-model representational similarity analyses.

The composite function vector experiment on one-shot analogies with untrained diagonal relations (above-left, etc.) is a genuinely interesting test of the linear representation hypothesis in a multimodal setting, and the code is publicly available. Limitations and potential misuse are discussed honestly in the limitations and impact statements.
weaknesses: Absolute performance numbers are very low for OpenFlamingo across all experiments (e.g., ~5-14% accuracy, sometimes barely above the zero-shot baseline), and the improvements over baselines are modest in absolute terms; the paper does not report statistical significance tests, error bars, or variance over seeds for any comparison, so claims that fine-tuned vectors 'significantly outperform' baselines are not formally supported.

The novelty is incremental: the core machinery (AIE head selection, mean activation averaging, zero-shot injection, and even the fine-tuning of task vectors via LoFit-style objectives) closely follows prior work (Todd et al., 2024; Jorgensen et al., 2023; Yin et al., 2024), with the main new elements being the application domain and the composite-vector analogy experiment.

Several potentially important methodological choices are under-justified: the injection layer is layer 19 for the synthetic dataset but layer 8 for GQA fine-tuning without explanation; there is no analysis of whether fine-tuned vectors still remain causally localized to the selected heads; and the effect size of the initial (untrained) FV over baselines is small in Figures 6 and 14, leaving the causal claim on shakier ground than the fine-tuning result.

The RSA analysis (Appendix G) reveals that OpenFlamingo's relation vectors are nearly collinear (pairwise cosine > 0.9), which raises questions about whether they encode distinct relations versus a generic 'task' direction; the paper reports this but does not reconcile it with the claimed relation-specific encoding.

The Qwen3-VL four-shot ICL baseline in the analogy experiment (Appendix E) is omitted due to GPU memory limitations, weakening the comparison for the headline CFV result on that model, and baseline prompting choices (e.g., whether ICL and FV use matched prompts/tokens) are not analyzed for confounds such as output-length bias in top-1 first-token matching.

Generalization claims rely on relatively narrow relation sets (4-7 spatial, 5 agentic relations) and the GQA filtering criteria heavily constrain images; the acknowledged narrowness limits how far the 'LMMs encode visual relational knowledge' conclusion can be pushed.

strengths: The paper successfully extends the function vector framework (Todd et al., 2024) from LLMs to large multimodal models for visual relations, a setting the authors plausibly argue has not yet been explored with this specific approach.

The methodology is systematic: causal mediation analysis to identify heads, zero-shot injection experiments, fine-tuning of vectors with a frozen backbone, ablations over injection layer, head-set size, and context size, plus appendices covering cross-dataset transfer and representational similarity across models.

The evaluation spans synthetic and real-image (GQA) datasets, two model families, spatial and agentic relations, and held-out object/relation generalization tests, which is broader than many interpretability studies.
Code is publicly released and dataset construction is documented in detail (Appendix A), supporting reproducibility.
The limitations section is honest, acknowledging the narrow relational vocabulary and the one-shot constraint of the composite-vector procedure.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the paper is a largely direct transposition of an established method (function vectors) to a new modality, closely following Multimodal Task Vectors (Huang et al., 2024) and Visual Task Vectors (Hojel et al., 2024), which already established vector-based task summaries in LMMs. The delta over these works needs sharper articulation.

Extremely low baseline accuracies (OpenFlamingo 4.8–9.7% zero-shot on Synthetic) cast doubt on whether the task measures relational reasoning at all for these models, or whether injected vectors exploit prompt-format and lexical biases. The paper does not control for frequency/co-occurrence priors, which could largely explain fine-tuned-vector gains (e.g., OpenFlamingo improving only from ~11% to 13.6%).

Missing critical baselines: the fine-tuned function vector is compared only against zero-shot/ICL prompting. There is no comparison against a random-vector fine-tuned control, prompt tuning, a linear probe on hidden states, or standard PEFT with a comparable parameter budget — all needed to claim the gains reflect extracted relational structure rather than cheap optimization of d-dimensional logits.

Evaluation protocol is underspecified and potentially ambiguous: top-1 accuracy against 'the first token of the target object label' is problematic when GQA images contain multiple objects instantiating the same relation (acknowledged in Appendix A), so multiple valid answers may exist. Chance levels are never stated; claims of being 'far below human levels' are made without any human experiment.

Statistical rigor is weak: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests anywhere; figures use inconsistent and truncated Y-axis scales (noted in the caption itself), which visually inflates differences between conditions.

The composite/analogy result supporting the linear representation hypothesis is thin: absolute accuracies are low (16.8% OpenFlamingo), only four diagonal compositions of already-trained axis relations are tested, and the connection to the linear representation hypothesis is asserted rather than analyzed (e.g., no geometric analysis of the vector subspace).

Appendix G (cross-model RSA being negative, r = −0.38/−0.29) undercuts the paper's generalization narrative — the 'relational geometry' is not shared across models — yet this finding is not discussed in the main text.

Some technical choices are asserted without justification, e.g., why the FV is a sum over top-head means (Eq. 2) rather than the per-head average used in prior work, and why different injection layers (19 vs. 8) are chosen for synthetic vs. GQA fine-tuning.

strengths: Extends the function vector framework (Todd et al., 2024) to large multimodal models, a natural but underexplored direction, and targets visual relations (spatial and agentic) rather than simple visual prompting tasks covered by prior visual/multimodal task vector work (Hojel et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2024)

Solid methodological pipeline: causal mediation analysis (AIE) to identify heads, zero-shot injection, fine-tuning of vectors with a frozen backbone, and composite vectors for one-shot analogies, each with a clearly stated hypothesis and evaluation protocol

Breadth of experiments: two LMMs (OpenFlamingo-4B, Qwen3-VL-4B), a controlled synthetic dataset and real-image GQA datasets, plus ablations over injection layer, head set size, and context size, cross-dataset transfer (Synthetic to GQA), novel-object generalization, and RSA/similarity analyses across models

The composite function vector experiments on untrained relations (above-left, above-right, etc.) are an interesting test of the linear representation hypothesis in multimodal settings, with clear improvements over ICL baselines (8.1% to 16.8%; 28.7% to 45.1%)
Honest limitations section identifying the narrow relation set and the contextual-demonstration dependency of composite vectors; code is publicly available
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the core machinery (AIE, top-k head selection, averaging activations, injection at intermediate layers) is directly transplanted from Todd et al., and the fine-tuning idea parallels LoFit (Yin et al., 2024); the contribution is primarily an application/adaptation to multimodal relation tasks

Absolute performance is very low in several conditions (e.g., OpenFlamingo FFV at 13.6% on novel objects; initial FVs sometimes near or below the 4-shot ICL baseline on GQA), which weakens the practical significance and complicates the claim that vectors 'encode' relational knowledge; no statistical significance tests, confidence intervals, or multiple-run variance are reported for any comparison

Missing stronger baselines: fine-tuning a single d-dimensional vector with a frozen model should be compared against matched-capacity alternatives such as prompt tuning, a learned soft prompt per relation, or sparse LoRA; without these it is unclear that FVs are the right (rather than merely convenient) representation

Inconsistencies that need clarification: fine-tuning injects at layer 19 for synthetic data but layer 8 for GQA, which sits oddly with the claimed intermediate-layer optimum (around layer 19) and the layer-effect analysis; Section 4.3 claims FFV is best across all seven spatial relations for OpenFlamingo, but the transfer figure (Figure 16) shows 4-shot ICL outperforming all FV conditions, an apparent tension that is not reconciled

The composite vector weighting scheme (Eq. 5) is ad hoc, and the analogy evaluation is limited to diagonal combinations of four cardinal relations with a single hand-designed source/target structure; no analysis of failure cases or of whether the weights recover the 'true' composition

Very low baseline accuracies for OpenFlamingo (4.8-9.7% on Synthetic) raise the question of whether the task is learnable by that model at all, weakening interpretability conclusions drawn from its interventions
Figures 6-7 show averaged results without error bars, and some y-axis scalings make effect sizes hard to compare; per-relation variance appears substantial in Appendix Figures 14-15
